opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Rare diseases are one of the areas where I think AI could matter most, partly because of how hard the problem is today. There are something like seven thousand rare diseases. Together they affect hundreds of millions of people around the world, but each one on its own might affect only a few thousand patients, or sometimes just a handful of families. That creates a very tough situation. There often isn't enough data, there aren't enough specialists, and there isn't enough commercial incentive to build a drug program around each condition one by one.

I see AI helping in a few places along that path.

The first is diagnosis. Many rare disease patients go through what people call a "diagnostic odyssey." It can take five, seven, sometimes ten years of seeing different doctors before anyone puts a name to what's going on. A lot of that delay is a pattern-recognition problem. The symptoms are spread across different specialties, and no single clinician has seen enough cases to spot the pattern. Models that can reason across clinical notes, genomic data, and the medical literature at once can suggest possibilities a busy physician might never think of. Even shortening that odyssey by a few years changes a family's life.

The second is understanding the biology. For many rare diseases we know the gene involved but not much about the mechanism. AI is getting quite good at helping researchers read across huge amounts of literature, generate hypotheses, interpret variants, and predict how a protein change might affect function. That speeds up the slow early work of figuring out what's actually going wrong.

The third, and maybe the most exciting, is changing the economics of drug development. If AI can help identify drug repurposing candidates, design molecules or genetic therapies faster, and make trials smarter even with very small patient populations, then the cost of working on a disease that affects five hundred people starts to look feasible. That's the real shift. These diseases have been neglected not because people don't care, but because the math didn't work. AI could change the math.

I'd add one important caveat. None of this replaces clinicians, researchers, or the patient communities themselves. In rare diseases, patient advocacy groups and families are often the ones holding the data, running the registries, and pushing the science forward. The best outcome is AI acting as a force multiplier for those people, so that a small foundation or a single dedicated lab can do what used to take a large pharmaceutical team.

So I'm genuinely optimistic. I think we're moving from a world where most rare diseases are essentially untouched to one where far more of them can at least get a real shot at a diagnosis and a treatment.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could identify drug-repurposing candidates, but does not state that these are already approved drugs or that AI identifies uses by reasoning from their mechanisms of action.

r002.rationale: The response is optimistic that AI could make more rare diseases eligible for diagnosis and treatment, but it does not say personalized treatments will soon be available at large scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about rare diseases is that the core problem has always been a numbers problem. There are something like seven thousand of them, and most affect so few people that the traditional drug development model simply doesn't work. You can't run a large trial, you can't justify the economics, and often there aren't even enough patients in one place for a specialist to build intuition.

AI changes that in a few concrete ways. The first is diagnosis. The average rare disease patient waits years and sees many doctors before getting a name for what they have. A model that has effectively read every case report and every genetics paper can recognize a pattern that no single clinician has seen before. That alone is transformative, because you can't treat what you haven't identified.

The second is the science itself. For a lot of these conditions we know the gene, we know the mutation, but the gap between that knowledge and a therapy has been enormous. Being able to reason about protein structure, to predict how a variant disrupts function, and to propose candidate molecules compresses work that used to take a lab a decade.

And the third, which I think is underappreciated, is that AI lowers the cost of trying. When one experiment or one analysis gets cheap enough, you can pursue a disease that affects fifty people, not just fifty thousand. That's the shift I'm most excited about. It's not one miracle cure. It's making the long tail of human suffering economically and scientifically addressable for the first time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses diagnosis, disease biology, and proposing candidate molecules, but does not say AI can find new rare-disease uses for already approved drugs by reasoning from their mechanisms.

r002.rationale: The response says lower costs could make research on very small patient groups feasible, but does not express that AI could soon enable personalized treatments at large scale.

astra-6.text:
I think AI could change what’s feasible for diseases that affect very small numbers of people. One of the challenges with rare diseases is that the evidence is scattered: a few patients at one hospital, a few at another, and research across different fields. AI could help researchers connect those pieces, identify possible causes, and prioritize treatments to investigate.

It could also help shorten the path to diagnosis by helping clinicians recognize patterns that are difficult to spot, especially when they’ve never encountered that condition before.

But finding a promising pattern isn’t the same as having a treatment. We still need careful experiments, clinical evidence, and close collaboration with patients. What excites me is the possibility of making that work faster and more practical, so that the number of people with a disease becomes less of a barrier to developing a treatment.

r001.rationale: It says AI could connect scattered evidence, identify possible causes, and prioritize treatments to investigate, but does not state that it can find new uses for approved drugs by reasoning from their mechanisms of action.

r002.rationale: It describes making treatment development faster and more practical, but does not express that personalized rare-disease treatments could soon be enabled at large scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could change what’s possible by helping us learn from very small amounts of data. With rare diseases, patients may be scattered around the world, and each clinician might see only one or two cases. AI could help connect those observations, recognize patterns, and give researchers better leads to investigate.

That could mean helping someone reach a diagnosis sooner, or identifying an existing drug that might be worth testing for a different disease. But finding a promising pattern isn’t the same as finding a treatment. We still need experiments, clinical evidence, and close collaboration with patients and physicians.

What makes me hopeful is the possibility that the number of people who have a disease becomes less of a barrier to making progress.

r001.rationale: The response mentions identifying an existing drug to test for another disease, but does not say AI reasons from drugs’ mechanisms of action.

r002.rationale: The response expresses hope that AI can help rare disease research, but does not state that it will soon enable personalized treatments at large scale.
